speaker_role: current admissions officers (Tulane international admission director, GW senior assistant director, Northeastern rep) plus a high school counselor
commercial_incentive: none evident; appears to be an outreach/recruiting webinar for international (India-focused) applicants, not a paid consulting service
key_insights: At Tulane, roughly 36,000 applications compete for 1,700 seats; about 18,000 are deemed academically qualified, but only 6-7,000 get offers, so most cuts happen on non-academic grounds
Institutional needs (new majors, new athletic programs, regional recruiting goals) can override individual merit in admit decisions, independent of a student's qualifications
Readers explicitly check whether both parents attended college to flag first-generation status, and treat this as a distinct evaluation factor
Predicted exam scores (e.g., UK A-level predictions) are not counted in review since they are not official, final results
In mock committee review, essays that read as a diary or simply state traits ('I am hardworking') are marked down versus essays that show specific experience

A school's financial aid policy for international students can flip a decision: a compelling low-income applicant may be denied by a no-need-based-aid school while a less remarkable domestic applicant is preferred
specific_numbers_or_facts: ~18,000 of Tulane's applicants judged academically qualified, but only 6,000-7,000 admitted (Darryl)
Northeastern has an institutional priority to admit/enroll students from the top 10% of their class (Darryl)
Fictional 'Harvest College' teaching profile used in the exercise: 20-25% acceptance rate, SAT middle 50% 1462-1540, ACT 32-34
notable_or_distinctive: runs a live, fairly transparent mock admissions-committee simulation on three real (anonymized) international applicants, showing how three different real universities would decide differently based on institutional aid policy and yield needs
reliability_notes: long freeform panel with cross-talk and some name/transcription garbling (e.g. 'Akshay' becomes 'a che'/'Ashay'); presenters explicitly caveat that the 'Harvest College' profile is fictional and real decisions vary by institution
